title: Experts stress early diagnosis and identifying underlying cause of anaemia
summary: Experts at a The Hindu webinar urged early diagnosis and investigation of underlying causes of anaemia rather than assuming iron deficiency. They highlighted diverse causes — including vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, inherited disorders, chronic disease and infections — and stressed tailored treatment, balanced nutrition, routine screening and avoiding self-medication with iron supplements.
content:
“Anaemia is not a disease by itself but a clinical finding that signals an underlying health condition. Identifying its cause is the first step towards effective treatment,” experts said during The Hindu's webinar titled 'Anaemia: Understanding Causes and Effects'.

The panel explained that while iron deficiency remains the most common cause of anaemia, the condition can also result from deficiencies of vitamin B12 or folate, inherited blood disorders such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease, chronic kidney disease, infections, autoimmune disorders, bone marrow diseases and several other underlying illnesses. Management, they said, should always be tailored to the underlying cause rather than assuming all anaemia is due to iron deficiency.

Ramya Uppuluri, consultant paediatric haematologist and oncologist at Apollo Hospitals, discussed anaemia in children and adolescents. She outlined nutritional and inherited causes, early warning signs, and the importance of timely diagnosis during the growing years. Uppuluri highlighted the role of adequate nutrition, early intervention and regular follow-up in preventing complications that could affect growth, development and learning.

Speaking on anaemia in adults, Divya M., consultant haematologist at Rela Hospital, described the investigations used to determine the underlying cause and reviewed advances in diagnosis and treatment. She explained that treatment should be guided by cause rather than relying solely on iron supplements, and highlighted newer diagnostic approaches and management options for complex blood disorders.

Subham Bhattacharya, consultant in haematology at CK Birla Hospitals, discussed advances in diagnosing and managing anaemia and emphasised the importance of recognising symptoms early and seeking appropriate medical care.

During the question-and-answer session, participants asked about iron deficiency without anaemia, persistent anaemia despite iron therapy, inherited blood disorders, the impact of anaemia on cognition and immunity, blood donation and iron stores, newer laboratory tests, and the need to strengthen public-health screening beyond simple haemoglobin estimation.

The experts cautioned against self-medication with iron supplements without medical evaluation and stressed that balanced nutrition, routine health screening, early diagnosis and evidence-based treatment are essential to reducing the burden of anaemia and preventing long-term complications.

The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dFBimIT8I-Q
